1.note: The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

Here David is using the possessive form **God of my praise** to describe God as the one whom he praises. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God whom I praise]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please do not be silent]

2.note: Here, **mouth** represents people who are speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [wicked and deceitful people speak against me]

Here, **tongue** represents the words that people speak. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [they speak untrue things concerning me]

3.note: Here, **words of hatred** represents people speaking hateful things. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and people surround me saying hateful things]

4.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **love**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Instead of loving me as I love them]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [they accuse me of doing bad things]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [but I turn to prayer] or [but I continue to pray]

5.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **evil** and **good**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [They do evil things to me although I did good things to them]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **hatred** and **love**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [and they hate me although I was loving to them]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they put hatred upon me in return for my love]

6.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please appoint a wicked one over him]

Here David is speaking as if God would **appoint** a human judge to preside over his enemy. He means that he wants God to bring judgment upon his enemy. If this image does not communicate well in your language, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Appoint a wicked one to judge him]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [a wicked man]

By **an accuser**, David means someone who will bring formal charges against his enemy in court. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and may someone accuse him before that wicked judge of doing evil things]

7.note: The expression **is judged** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [When the wicked one judges him]

David is using **may he come out guilty** as a common expression of his culture to mean “may the verdict be that he is guilty.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may the verdict be that he is guilty]

This could mean: (1) The enemy is praying to Yahweh and since his prayer is insincere, Yahweh should count it as sinful. Alternate translation: [and may his prayer be considered as another sin] or (2) The enemy is pleading with the judge, and the judge should count his plea as a further offense. Alternate translation: [and may his plea be considered as an offense]

8.note: David is using **May his days be few** as a common expression of his culture to mean “May he die soon” or “May he live only a short time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May he live only a short time]

Here David is speaking of a person’s role or authority as if it were a **position** that someone could physically occupy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may another take his authority] or [may another replace him]

9.note: David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and may his wife be a widow]

10.note: David is repeating forms of the verb **wander** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [And may his children wander far away]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and beg and seek for food]

By **their desolations**, David means their ruined homes or destroyed dwellings. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [from their destroyed houses]

11.note: Here David is speaking as if a creditor were a hunter or trapper who could **snare** the enemy’s possessions. He means that the creditor should seize or take control of everything the enemy owns. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May a creditor take]

David is using **all that is to him** as a common expression of his culture to mean “everything that belongs to him.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [everything that belongs to him]

The implication is that **his work** refers to the things that he worked for or the results of his labor. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the things that he worked for]

12.note: David is using **May there not be to him** as a common expression of his culture to mean “May he not have.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May he not have]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [someone who is kindly loyal to him]

The implication is that these would be children who have lost their father due to the curse pronounced against him in the previous verses. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [someone who pities his orphaned children]

13.note: David is using **be to cut off** as a common expression of his culture to mean “die” or “be destroyed.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May his posterity be destroyed]

The expression **may their name be blotted out** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [may you blot out their name]

Here David is speaking of making people be forgotten as if their names were written words that could be erased or **blotted out**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may there be no one bearing their name] or [may no one remember their name]

14.note: The expression **be remembered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh keep in mind the sin of his fathers] or [May you remember the sin of his fathers]
David is using the term **fathers** to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his ancestors]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and may the offense of his mother not be blotted out]

The expression **not be blotted out** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [and do not blot out the offense of his mother]

David is using **not be blotted out** as a common expression of his culture to mean “not be forgiven.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the offense of his mother not be forgiven]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **offense**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the things that his mother did that offended Yahweh not be blotted out]

15.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the sins of the enemy’s father and mother mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [May those sins be before Yahweh continually]

Here David is speaking of the sins as if they were objects that could be continually placed **before Yahweh** for him to see. He means he wants Yahweh to notice those sins. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh continually consider them]

David is using **cut off their remembrance** as a common expression of his culture to mean “destroy anything that would cause people to remember them.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and may he destroy anything that would cause people to remember them]

The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh, while the pronoun **their** refers to David’s enemies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and may he cut off any remembrance of those people]

Here, **the earth** represents any people living on earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from any people living on earth]

16.note: The pronoun **he** refers to David’s enemy. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [that man never remembered]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to be kind to others]

Here David is speaking of the man’s treatment of vulnerable people as if he **pursued** them like a hunter chasing prey. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but harassed]

David is not referring to specific **humble** and **needy** and **dejected** people. He means people who were humble and needy and dejected in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people who were humble and needy and dejected in heart]

David is using the adjectives **needy** and **dejected** as nouns to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [and needy people and people dejected in their hearts]

Here David is speaking of people as if their emotions were located in their **heart**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and those who felt very sad]
The implication is that he pursued these people until they died. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [until they died]

17.note: Here David is speaking as if cursing were an object that physically **came to** someone. He means that the person experienced the effects or consequences of cursing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and now those curses have fallen on him] or [and now I wish those bad things to happen to him]

David is emphasizing a negative meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with a mild expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the negative meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [and he hated blessing]

Here David is speaking as if blessing were an object that could be physically **far from** his enemy. He means that his enemy will not receive any blessing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will not receive any]

18.note: Here David is speaking of his enemy as if **cursing** were **his garment** that he put on. He means that cursing other people was habitual for this person, like clothing that someone wears regularly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he cursed other people continually]

David is making a comparison between **it entered into his inner being like water** and how deeply cursing has become part of his enemy’s character. The point of this comparison is that just as **water** penetrates thoroughly into a person when they drink, so **cursing** has penetrated deeply into this man’s inner being. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and it became a part of him like water does when we drink it]

David is making a comparison between how oil soaks into bones and how cursing has become part of his enemy’s inner being. The point of this comparison is that just as **oil** penetrates deeply and becomes absorbed, so cursing has become deeply absorbed into the enemy’s very nature. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and it became a part of him like oil would after it had entered into his bones]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and it entered into his inner being like oil penetrating his bones]

19.note: David is making a comparison between curses and **clothing** that someone wears. The point of this comparison is that just as **clothing** clings closely to a person’s body, so the curses should cling closely to his enemy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [May it wrap itself tightly to him like the clothing that he wears]

The pronoun **it** refers to the cursing mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [May that cursing be to him like the clothing that he wears]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and may it be for him like the belt]

David is making a comparison. The point of this comparison is that just as **the belt** is something that a person wears constantly, so the curse should cling to his enemy constantly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and may it always be around him as the belt]

It might seem that the expression **he always girds himself with it** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [he always girds himself with] or [with which he always girds himself]

20.note: The pronoun **This** refers to the curse that David has been describing in the previous verses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [May the effects of this curse be]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [May the effects of this curse be]

Here, **This, the payment** could mean: (1) David is asking Yahweh that this be the payment to his accusers. Alternate translation: [May this be the payment] or (2) David is stating that this is the payment to his accusers. Alternate translation: [This will be the payment]

Here David is speaking of God’s punishment as if it were **payment** that God gives to David’s accusers. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [This, the punishment of my accusers from Yahweh]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and may this be the payment from Yahweh to those speaking evil against my soul]

Here, **soul** represents the entire person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and those speaking evil against me]

21.note: By **do with me**, David means “treat me kindly” or “act favorably toward me.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [do good to me] or [do what I ask]

Here, **name** represents who God is or God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [on account of your character]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Because you are good and faithful to your covenant]

22.note: The terms **poor** and **needy** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [I am very poor]

Here David is speaking of his emotional distress as if his **heart breaks** physically. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am in great despair]

23.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a shadow when it lengthens** quickly disappears, so David’s life is quickly passing away. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Like how quickly a shadow disappears as it lengthens]

The expression **I am made to go** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I will leave]

The expression **I am shaken off** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I will fall off like a locust]

David is making a comparison. The point of this comparison is that just as **a locust** is easily shaken off, so David is easily dismissed or removed from his position. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I will disappear as quickly as someone shakes off a locust]

24.note: Here, **knees** represents the strength of the whole body. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [My body is weak]

The word **from** indicates that **fasting** is the reason for the weakness described in the first part of the verse. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that the fasting is the cause of the weakness. Alternate translation: [because of fasting very much]

By **my flesh is gaunt from fatness**, David means that his flesh is gaunt from the complete absence of fat. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and my flesh is gaunt, very far from being fat]

25.note: The pronoun **I** is stated twice here for emphasis. David is emphasizing his own condition or state in contrast to his enemies. If a speaker of your language would use explicit pronouns for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [As for me, I am]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **disgrace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I am disgusting to them]

Here the word that is translated **they see me** does not clearly indicate when the action of seeing occurs. It could mean “whenever they see me” or refer to a specific instance. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [whenever they see me]

The expression **shake their head** describes a symbolic action by which people showed contempt or mockery. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [they show that they despise me by shaking their heads]

26.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please help me]

The psalmist is not using the phrase **my God** to mean that he possesses or controls Yahweh, but rather to emphasize that Yahweh is the God he worships as modeled in the UST. See the introduction to Psalms for further discussion.

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [according to your covenant to be faithful]

By **according to your covenant faithfulness**, David means according to God’s promise to be faithful to his people. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [since you have promised to be faithful to me]

27.note: Here, **so that** marks **they know that this is your hand; you, Yahweh, you have done it** as the goal or purpose of “Help me, Yahweh my God; save me according to your covenant faithfulness” in the previous verse. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [because I want them to know]
The pronoun **they** refers to David’s accusers. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [so that the people who accuse me know]

Here, **hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that this is your doing]

David is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you have done it** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh is the one who has acted. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [it is you, Yahweh, who have done it]

The pronoun **it** refers to Yahweh saving David, as he asked Yahweh to do in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [you, Yahweh, are the one who saved me]

28.note: The pronoun **They** refers to David’s accusers. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The people who accuse me, they will curse]

David is stating the pronouns **they** and **you** separately for emphasis, even though the verbs translated as **they will curse** and **you will bless** already include their meanings. He is doing that to create a strong contrast between what his enemies will do (curse) and what God will do (bless). If a speaker of your language would use explicit pronouns for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [They are the ones who will curse, but you are the one who will bless]

By **they arise**, David means they arise to attack him. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [they arise to attack me]

The psalmist is speaking of himself in the third person as **your servant** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [and I, your servant]

29.q: יִלְבְּשׁ֣וּ שׂוֹטְנַ֣⁠י כְּלִמָּ֑ה וְ⁠יַעֲט֖וּ כַ⁠מְעִ֣יל בָּשְׁתָּֽ⁠ם
29.note: These two phrases **May my accusers be clothed with disgrace** and **may they wear their shame like a robe** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [May my accusers be clothed with shameful disgrace as though it were a robe]

Here David is speaking of his accusers as if they were people who could be **clothed with disgrace**. He means that their disgrace should be clearly seen and obvious to everyone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May it be obvious how disgraceful my accusers are]

David is making a comparison between **their shame** and **a robe**. The point of this comparison is that just as a robe is visible to everyone who sees the person wearing it, so David wants his accusers’ shame to be visible and obvious to everyone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [may their shame be so obvious to everyone that it is like a robe that they are wearing]

30.note: Here, **mouth** represents speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will speak to greatly thank Yahweh]

David is using the adjective **many** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and in the midst of many people]

31.note: Here David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a person who could physically **stand at the right hand of the needy**. The image of standing at someone’s right hand means to be ready to help and defend them. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [he advocates for the needy] or [he helps the needy]

David is using the adjective **needy** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [needy people]

By **the judges of his soul**, David means those who seek to condemn him to death. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [from officials who want to take his life]
